strengths: Addresses a genuine practical pain point (expensive per-scene contrastive training) with a fully training-free pipeline, and reports substantial reductions in CLIP feature storage (~1000x) and peak VRAM relative to baselines.

Strong quantitative results: outperforms prior training-based point-level and even several pixel-based methods on LERF object selection (by ~10.7 mIoU) and on ScanNet semantic segmentation across 19/15/10-class settings.

The neutral point processing module (multi-view semantic entropy combined with geometric opacity filtering) is a sensible, lightweight mechanism for handling boundary ambiguity and is validated with a clear ablation (Table 4).

The idea of distilling multi-view CLIP image feature inconsistency into a single canonical textual representation via a VLM (Section 3.3) is a reasonable and reasonably novel engineering solution to viewpoint variance, supported by an ablation comparing it against single-view, averaged, and IoU-filtered image-matching baselines (Table 5).
The paper is generally clearly written and includes useful comparative tables (training time, storage, VRAM) that make the efficiency argument concrete and easy to evaluate.
weaknesses: The central 'polysemy' claim, heavily emphasized in the abstract and introduction (e.g., a desk point being simultaneously 'desk,' 'wooden,' and 'furniture'), is never directly validated by an experiment; no benchmark or qualitative case specifically demonstrates multi-concept assignment to the same Gaussian, leaving this key contribution largely unsubstantiated by evidence.

The framework is a pipeline built almost entirely from off-the-shelf components (SAM, DAM2SAM tracker, Gemini 2.5 Pro VLM, CLIP), so the technical novelty is incremental engineering/integration rather than a fundamentally new representation or algorithm; the object-grouping and neutral-point ideas, while useful, are relatively simple heuristics layered on existing tools.

Reliance on a closed, proprietary VLM (Gemini 2.5 Pro) for the core semantic distillation step raises reproducibility concerns (API cost, version drift, potential non-determinism); despite the claim of being 'VLM-agnostic,' no experiments substitute an open-source VLM to substantiate this robustness claim.

The efficiency narrative ('hours to minutes') is only partially supported: Table 1 reports CLIP feature storage and peak VRAM but omits total end-to-end wall-clock time for the full pipeline (SAM mask generation across granularities, DAM2SAM tracking, periodic re-detection, and VLM querying per object), which could be non-trivial and should be reported for a fair efficiency comparison.

No sensitivity analysis or reported values for the fixed thresholds (τh, τα, η) used across all experiments; given these thresholds directly gate the neutral-point exclusion and query matching, their robustness across differing scene types/datasets is unverified.

Limitations section is brief and does not address potential failure modes tied to VLM hallucination/misnaming at scale, nor quantify how often such errors occur, despite this being flagged as a limitation.

Comparisons are limited to LERF and ScanNet; broader scene diversity (e.g., outdoor/driving scenes mentioned as a motivating application) is not evaluated, somewhat narrowing the demonstrated generality of the method relative to its stated motivations.

strengths: The paper identifies three concrete and well-motivated limitations of prior 3DGS open-vocabulary methods (expensive per-scene optimization, monosemous assignment, and fragile multi-view CLIP feature aggregation) and designs targeted solutions for each, giving the work a clear conceptual narrative.

The training-free design is a meaningful practical contribution: Table 1 shows dramatic reductions in per-scene adaptation time (hours to none), CLIP feature storage (~3GB to ~3MB), and peak VRAM, which is valuable for real-world deployment.

Strong empirical results: the method outperforms multiple recent training-based baselines (OpenGaussian, InstanceGaussian, Dr.Splat, LangSplat, etc.) by sizable margins on both the LERF object-selection benchmark (+10.7 mIoU over the best prior method) and ScanNet semantic segmentation across three class splits.

The neutral point processing idea (combining multi-view semantic entropy with geometric opacity to identify and discard boundary-ambiguous Gaussians) is a sensible, lightweight mechanism, and the ablation in Table 4 shows both entropy and opacity filtering are complementary and necessary.

The VLM-based semantic distillation strategy (converting volatile multi-view visual CLIP features into a canonical textual representation) is an interesting and well-motivated alternative to naive multi-view feature averaging, and the ablation in Table 5 convincingly shows its advantage over single-view, averaged, and filtered image-matching baselines.

The paper provides fairly comprehensive experimental coverage across two distinct benchmarks/tasks (LERF object selection, ScanNet semantic segmentation) with both quantitative and qualitative comparisons, plus a resource-cost table that contextualizes the efficiency gains.
weaknesses: The central 'polysemy' claim, prominently featured in the abstract, introduction, and title framing (a Gaussian being simultaneously 'desk,' 'wooden,' and 'furniture'), is never directly evaluated. There is no dedicated experiment, metric, or qualitative example demonstrating that the method actually assigns and correctly retrieves multiple simultaneous semantic labels per point; all reported benchmarks (LERF selection, ScanNet segmentation) are effectively single-label retrieval tasks, leaving this headline contribution unsubstantiated by evidence.

The pipeline depends on a closed, proprietary VLM (Gemini 2.5 Pro) accessed presumably via API for generating object identity hypotheses. This raises reproducibility concerns (model behavior can drift or become unavailable) and the paper does not report the VLM's contribution to total pipeline latency/cost, which undermines the completeness of the 'minutes not hours' efficiency claim in Table 1 (only training time, storage, and VRAM are reported, not the full inference-time pipeline cost including SAM segmentation, DAM2SAM tracking, and VLM calls).

The method is a combination of several existing off-the-shelf components (SAM, DAM2SAM, a general VLM, CLIP), and the individual technical contributions (weighted back-projection, entropy/opacity-based neutral point filtering, VLM-based text distillation) are each relatively incremental engineering choices; the novelty lies mainly in the overall training-free pipeline design rather than in a new representation or algorithmic principle.

Two fixed thresholds (τh for entropy, τα for opacity) are used across all experiments, but there is no sensitivity analysis or discussion of how these were chosen or how robust results are to their values across different scene types/datasets.

The comparison set consists exclusively of training-based baselines; no other training-free or matching-based 3D open-vocabulary method is discussed or compared against, making it unclear how this approach positions against any prior zero-shot alternatives (if they exist) versus purely against the training-based paradigm.

The failure/limitation discussion is brief and largely qualitative (SAM mask errors, occasional VLM mislabeling) without quantitative failure-case analysis or error breakdowns, which would strengthen understanding of the method's practical robustness.

strengths: Well-motivated reformulation of 3D open-vocabulary understanding: the 'extrinsic paradigm' that decouples geometry (Gaussian points) from semantics (object-level text indices) directly targets three concretely articulated flaws of the dominant embedding paradigm (geometry-semantic inconsistency at boundaries, storage bloat, and single-vector semantic rigidity/polysemy).

The neutral-point identification mechanism (multi-view semantic entropy + opacity filtering) is a sensible, well-ablated technical contribution for handling ambiguous boundary points, an issue often glossed over in prior work.

Training-free design combined with VLM-based textual grounding of object groups is efficient: the paper convincingly demonstrates orders-of-magnitude reduction in feature storage (GB to MB) and VRAM (Table 1), which is a genuinely useful practical contribution.

Broad empirical validation: LERF object selection, ScanNet semantic segmentation, extensive ablations (neutral-point thresholds, VLM choice, number of prompts, sparse-mask robustness), qualitative editing demonstrations (removal/translation/stylization), and additional real-world/GraspNet tests show the authors stress-tested the method across settings.

Good failure-case and diagnostic analysis (Sec. 9-10), including visualization of CLIP feature inconsistency across viewpoints and quantification of multi-label polysemy in ScanNet scenes, which strengthens the paper's motivating claims with direct evidence rather than assertion alone.
Clear component-wise runtime/VRAM breakdown (Table 9) improves transparency about where computational cost is spent.
weaknesses: Overclaiming of SOTA status on the LERF object-selection benchmark: Table 2 shows several embedding-based methods (LAGA 65.6, 3DVLGS 62.0, Occam's LGS 61.3) substantially outperform the proposed method (54.3 mean mIoU); the paper's claimed '3.9 mIoU' improvement is only relative to the training-free category (LUDVIG), not the overall best baseline. The abstract's statement that the method 'outperforms established embedding-based frameworks' is therefore only partially true and should be scoped more precisely.

The method depends on a proprietary, closed VLM (Gemini 2.5 Pro) for the core semantic grounding step, raising reproducibility concerns; Table 6 shows large accuracy swings (47.0 to 54.3 mIoU) depending on which VLM is used, meaning reported numbers are tied to a specific, non-open model whose behavior may change or be inaccessible to others.

Scalability of the object-level grouping pipeline to scenes with many more objects/instances is not analyzed quantitatively; the reported 9.25-minute processing time is for a scene with 131 categories, and per-object independent tracking, backward matching, and VLM querying could grow expensive for larger or more cluttered real-world scenes (only qualitative, small-scale real-world/GraspNet examples are shown, without quantitative metrics).

Pipeline relies on several hand-tuned, fixed hyperparameters (e.g., re-detection interval Δt=10, τ_area=0.9, τ_iou=0.6, entropy/opacity thresholds) that are fixed across all experiments; while some sensitivity analysis is given for the neutral-point thresholds, the sensitivity of the object-tracking heuristics themselves is less thoroughly justified.

Object editing capability (Sec. 7.3) and real-world generalization (Sec. 7.4) are demonstrated only qualitatively without any quantitative evaluation, limiting the strength of these claimed use cases.

The multi-granularity/polysemy claim, a headline motivation of the paper, is supported mainly by qualitative examples and a post-hoc statistical analysis (Fig. 13) rather than a dedicated quantitative benchmark measuring polysemy-handling accuracy against baselines.
